events.title: The death of Pope Clement V
events.shortBlurb: Thirty-three days after Jacques de Molay's burning, the pope who suppressed the Templars died at Roquemaure…
body: On 20 April 1314 Pope Clement V died at Roquemaure on the Rhône — thirty-three days after the last Grand Master of the Temple, Jacques de Molay, had gone to the stake in Paris. Later chroniclers told how Molay, from the flames, summoned pope and king to answer before God's tribunal within the year; the tale is not in the earliest witnesses, but Philip the Fair indeed followed Clement to the grave that November.

Bertrand de Got, archbishop of Bordeaux, had been elected on 5 June 1305, after a conclave of eleven months, and crowned at Lyon; he never entered Italy, and in 1309 he settled the papal court at Avignon, beginning the seventy years' sojourn of the papacy on French soil.

Under the shadow of the French king he convened the Council of Vienne (1311–12), which suppressed the Order of the Temple by the bull Vox in excelso of 22 March 1312 and gave its goods to the Hospitallers; his constitutions, the Clementinae, issued by his successor, stood in the law of the Church for centuries. After his death the cardinals wrangled more than two years before choosing John XXII in August 1316.

events.title: The execution of Elizabeth Barton
events.shortBlurb: The Holy Maid of Kent, whose visions condemned the king's divorce, was hanged at Tyburn without trial…
body: On 20 April 1534 Elizabeth Barton, the Benedictine nun called the Holy Maid of Kent, was drawn from the Tower to Tyburn and hanged for treason, with five companions — her confessor Edward Bocking, her parish priest Richard Masters, and the Observant friars Richard Risby and Hugh Rich among them — condemned not by any jury but by act of Parliament.

A servant at Aldington in Kent, she had fallen into trances in 1525, and her revelations, judged sincere by a commission of Archbishop Warham, made her famous; professed at St. Sepulchre's, Canterbury, she was consulted by the great, Bishop Fisher and Sir Thomas More among them. When Henry VIII put aside Catherine of Aragon for Anne Boleyn, the Maid prophesied that the king would die a villain's death and lose his realm within a month.

Cromwell broke her circle in 1533, and she was attainted by statute, about twenty-eight years old. On the scaffold, the chronicle relates, she owned herself the cause of her companions' deaths, 'and yet not so much to be blamed, considering that I was a simple woman.' Their heads were set on London Bridge and the gates of the city.
